BREAKING: The "AI Big 10" now accounts for a record 42% of US stock market cap.

This includes Magnificent 7 stocks as well as Broadcom, $AVGO, AMD, $AMD, and Micron, $MU.

This figure has more than doubled since the 2022 bear market low.

By comparison, during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble, the Technology, Media & Telecom (TMT) sector peaked at 41%, while the Nifty Fifty peaked at 40% in the 1970s.

Furthermore, Japan’s equity market bubble in the 1980s peaked at 44%.

In the past, only railroad stocks have significantly exceeded this concentration, accounting for 63% of US market cap at their highest point in the 1900s.

The dominance of Big Tech is extraordinary.

a16z's Alex Immerman, David George, and Sarah Wang on why a data center can lower your electricity bill:

"It may seem counterintuitive, but a data center can help lower your electricity rate. A recent US study showed that for every 10% increase in data center capacity, residential rates went down by 40 bps."

"You should think about it as a power grid is a shared fixed cost base: poles, wires, substations. A large stable customer, like a data center, can help spread those costs across more units of electricity. Simply put, more demand across a shared system is a positive."

"Investment in shared infrastructure can also improve the economics for the households and businesses connected to it."

"There's real examples of that today. It's not just lip service."

Still, 56% of Texas voters say more data centers would raise their power bills.

The catch is it depends on who pays. When developers cover their own grid upgrades instead of pushing them onto everyone else's bills, the savings are real.

a16z's @rmcentush on how to get that right: https://t.co/TobsqsZJq9

@aleximm @DavidGeorge83 @sarahdingwang

BREAKING: Global central banks acquired +39 tonnes of gold in August, marking their 5th consecutive monthly purchase.

This follows +23 tonnes in July and +52 tonnes in June.

China again led demand, adding +20 tonnes and bringing its year-to-date purchases to +80 tonnes.

China’s official gold reserves have now risen to a record 2,387 tonnes, or 9% of its total FX reserves.

Furthermore, Poland bought +8 tonnes, lifting its year-to-date purchases to +98 tonnes and total gold reserves to a record 648 tonnes.

So far in 2026, central banks have acquired +170 tonnes of gold.

Central banks continue to aggressively accumulate gold.

We're excited to invest in Preference Model.

Building RL environments that actually work is harder than it looks. Models are relentless at reward hacking, finding shortcuts, and exploiting vulnerabilities.

@preferencemodel has focused on the domain that matters most to labs right now: AI research and ML engineering itself.

Over the past year, the team has built RL environments for leading labs. Their focus has been on building the infrastructure to make harder, more resistant environments as models improve: tooling that finds where models are weak, generates new tasks to target those gaps, and tests environments against agents actively trying to break it.

This week they're open-sourcing Karotte, the framework they've used in production — hardened through more than a million evaluation runs and red-teaming.

We're thrilled to partner with @chem_safety and @Ning_Catsnail and the Preference Model team as they build the training grounds for capable and aligned models.

By @JenniferHli

BREAKING: Since the start of 2025, US jobs numbers have now been revised down in 16 out of 20 months by a total of -793,000 jobs.

This means that, on average, -39,650 jobs have been revised out of previously reported data each month during this period.

The most recent August and July jobs numbers were revised down by a total of -60,000.

Revisions to nonfarm payrolls have consistently occurred since the start of 2023.

If we apply this average to the +29,000 jobs add in September's report, it would imply a -10,650 contraction in nonfarm payrolls last month.

This would also mark their 3rd monthly decline of 2026, following a -156,000 drop in February and -10,000 in July.

What is happening here?

Executives in the Financials sector are turning cautious:

The unique seller/buyer ratio for Financials stood at 2.10x above its long-term average in Q3 2026, the highest reading across all major sectors.

This ratio compares the number of individual insiders who sold shares with the number who bought, regardless of how many times they sold.

The number of financial executives buying their own stocks in the sector fell to its lowest level in almost 23 years, while the number of sellers was not unusually high.

Energy and Technology followed, with ratios of 1.30x and 1.24x, respectively.

At the same time, the broader market seller/buyer ratio stood at 1.20x its long-term average last quarter, or 20% above the historical norm.

On the other hand, Consumer Staples had the lowest reading at just 0.50x, followed by Utilities at 0.55x and Materials at 0.57x.

Insider confidence is fading across key market sectors.

Commodity volatility keeps exploding, and the banks that walked away are scrambling back in.

30-day vol on the Bloomberg Commodity Index has had three major spikes since 2020: COVID, the Russia-Ukraine invasion that pushed it to roughly 34, and now the US-Iran war. Regional US banks are suddenly back offering commodity hedging because the price swings, and the fees, are too big to ignore.

When banks pile back into a business they abandoned, it tells you the quiet era is over. Serial supply shocks have turned commodities back into a volatility asset. That cuts both ways: real diversification for a portfolio, and real risk for anyone who is not hedged.

Oura tried to IPO at a $15.6 billion valuation last month and couldn't find the buyers. So it pulled the deal.

It sold itself as a health-data platform. Investors saw a company that still makes 80% of its money selling one gadget. Single-product companies that went public from 2005 to 2024 lost 32% on average after five years while the market gained 49%.

The market pays a platform multiple for recurring revenue and a hardware multiple for hardware. When a one-product company calls itself a platform, make it prove the subscriptions are real before you pay up for the story.

France now borrows for 10 years at almost the same yield as Italy and Greece, around 4.5%.

For two decades France was the safe core of Europe while those two were the risk trade. That gap has closed. The market has repriced France from core to periphery after decades of deficits and a budget it has not balanced since 1974.

Once lenders stop treating your debt as safe, every new deficit costs more and the math only gets harder. France is the test case for every developed country running deficits forever.

Diesel just hit a record $8.44 a gallon in parts of California.

Call it what it is: a supply shock. Refined products can't get out of the Middle East after the war knocked out refining runs, and the US is one of the only places left exporting diesel. Los Angeles is above $8 and the national average keeps climbing.

Diesel moves freight, farming and factories, so a spike like this taxes the real economy while broad prices stay calm. The other side of the trade is refiners, and their margins are going vertical.

DUKE reached a proposed settlement with NC utility consumer advocates and other stakeholders on new large-load rules, though still subject to regulator approval.

>50MW customers signing ESAs after 6/1/26 would face upfront payments for dedicated infrastructure plus deposits/collateral for shared transmission upgrades.
>WYFI going from ~54MW to 99MW at NC1 likely unaffected.
>WYFI NC1’s potential additional 200MW could be more expensive, with upfront infrastructure payments plus collateral for transmission upgrades.
>NC2/3 likely fall under the new rules as well, depending on how they’re structured. Each expansion is initially expected to be ~30MW, so could potentially fall below the 50MW threshold.

Added clarity could ultimately be positive for $WYFI. Regulator decision expected by mid-November, just after the election; supports hypothesis that election will unclog some stalled projects.

tweets.text:
Thanks for engaging, Balaji. 

The DoorDash point is a continuation of a theme I've been writing about for a while (in my Deep Dives and, more recently, on autonomous delivery), which is probably why I didn't spell it out again here. I intended it to be a narrower claim than you may have interpreted. Yes, DoorDash's international footprint was largely bought. My point is about new verticals at home, where DoorDash has shown a greater willingness to build while Uber has tended to buy.

On 2022-24, you're obviously right that Uber didn't deploy much in that window. But it deployed a good chunk on either side of it: Careem, Postmates, Drizly, Cornershop and Transplace before, and SpotHero, Getir, Delivery Hero and now ezCater after. Uber's own capital allocation framework earmarks roughly half of FCF for uses other than capital return, so I assumed that pattern may continue rather than 2022-24 to be the norm.

On ezCater, I take the point that order size matters. But the larger tickets allegedly come with half the commission, and we don't know the exact take rate. The press release said the business is profitable on a non-GAAP basis, which presumably means it isn't on a GAAP basis. There may well be meaningful synergies, and it may be accretive on a margin basis once restructuring costs are excluded. The release just didn't give much clarity on such synergy or the margin profile.

Finally, I'm certainly not suggesting Uber is Expedia. Uber's 2022-25 bottom line CAGR likely reflects a low starting base too. More importantly, the point I was really trying to land is simpler: it's not easy for investors to judge a bunch of acquisitions and underwrite a return profile on that capital. Organic reinvestment is relatively easier to underwrite; with M&A, you need a separate view on every deal, and the answers may take years to emerge. I'm not claiming these are destined to be bad investments... just that they're harder to underwrite, and the outcome of such capital allocation will matter a LOT for long-term shareholders in terms of whether the stock compounds at an attractive rate over the next 5-10 years.
